scope.flow: redeem() and swap() base-token payout paths in Covenant
scope.environment: Covenant contract with ERC20 base token; standard ERC20 self-transfer treated as no-op

statements.text: A user sets the payout recipient parameter to the Covenant contract address (address(this)) during redeem() or a base-out swap().
The base token is a standard ERC20 implementation that treats a self-transfer as a no-op, leaving the token balance unchanged.
In redeem(), the contract updates ms.baseSupply = localBaseSupply - amountOut - protocolFees and then executes safeTransfer to the user-specified recipient.
In swap() when assetOut == BASE, the contract updates ms.baseSupply = localBaseSupply - amount - protocolFees and then executes safeTransfer to the user-specified recipient.
The redeem() and swap() payout paths do not validate that the recipient is not the contract itself, unlike collectProtocolFee() which reverts on recipient == address(this).

When the recipient is address(this), baseSupply is decremented by the payout amount plus protocol fees while no base tokens actually leave the contract, creating a persistent divergence between actual balance and internal accounting.
The excess base tokens become permanently stranded, not reflected in internal accounting and not withdrawable through normal user flows or protocol fee collection.
Locked funds reduce effective liquidity available to all users because liquidity calculations rely on baseSupply rather than the actual token balance, potentially impairing future redemptions.
Inferred: base-token payouts in redeem() and swap() should reject a recipient equal to the contract itself so that accounting decrements correspond to tokens actually leaving the contract.
Materializing significant impact requires the triggering user to sacrifice their own redemption proceeds by locking their own tokens.

ambiguities: Report does not establish a concrete prior transaction or observed incident; trigger is conditional on a user choosing address(this) as recipient.
Whether the base token in any deployed market actually treats self-transfer as a no-op is not verified, only stated as typical.
Exact magnitude of stranded funds and liquidity degradation is not quantified.
